extracted.intended_audience: general readers and prospective Twitch users/streamers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, policies, and platform-level feature/monetization constraints and guidance relevant to producing and operating live streams and channels on Twitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age restrictions (Terms of Service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch's Terms of Service does not allow people under 13 years of age to use its services. Additionally, people who are at least 13 years old but below the age of majority in their jurisdiction may only use the services under the supervision or permission of a parent or other legal guardian who agrees to abide to the Terms of Service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hard eligibility requirement for account ownership/use; streamers and viewers must comply with age limits and parental supervision where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription price and revenue sharing for partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscribers can subscribe to partnered streamers' channels for US$4.99 a month. Twitch retains US$2.49 of [the subscription fee].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partners share in advertisement revenue and subscribers receive channel-specific perks (unique emoticons, chat privileges, etc.). The page also describes that most streamers get a 50% subscription revenue share, while some larger streamers historically had 70% premium terms (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription revenue split and premium thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Though most streamers get 50% of revenue from subscriptions, some larger streamers have premium subscription terms giving them 70% of subscription revenue. In a change announced in September 2022, premium streamers would keep 70% of the first $100,000 earned from subscriptions, after which their cut would be lowered to 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a contractual/monetization standard that affects streamer income and has been a point of controversy; streamers should expect variability and potential changes in splits over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emote slots allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch partnered broadcasters unlock more 'emote slots' as they gain more subscribers up to a maximum of 50 emotes per channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel growth (subscriber counts) determines available emote capacity; emotes are a partner perk and part of channel subscriber offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: VOD/archive retention limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The option to archive complete broadcasts on an indefinite basis ('save forever') was removed, meaning that they can only be retained for a maximum of 14 days, or 60 for partners and Turbo subscribers. Compiled highlights can be archived indefinitely, but they were limited to two hours in length (at introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators need to plan around limited automatic retention windows; highlights can be used for longer-term archival but have length limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright fingerprinting on archived clips
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch introduced a copyright fingerprinting system that would mute audio in archived clips if it detected a copyrighted song in the stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should avoid unlicensed copyrighted music in streams if they want audio retained in archives; otherwise audio may be muted in VODs/clips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulcasting and exclusivity contractual restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, Twitch enforced exclusivity agreements prohibiting partners/affiliates from streaming on other platforms. The platform previously noted that simulcasting on Twitch and other 'Twitch-like' streaming platforms was prohibited, with an exemption applied to short-form platforms such as Instagram and TikTok. In August 2022 Twitch announced it would no longer enforce its exclusivity agreement, and later (TwitchCon 2023) announced that streamers under an affiliation or partnership agreement (unless contractually required) would be allowed to simulcast on competing platforms such as YouTube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a streamer can simulcast or work for multiple platforms depends on contractual terms and evolving Twitch policy; streamers with exclusivity/premium deals should check contract details (including any platform-specific hourly obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branded content / sponsor placement restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch announced restrictions on third-party sponsor placements, including restricting the size of sponsor logos and prohibiting 'burned-in' audio, video, or display advertising. The policy was quickly retracted and clarified, stating it was intended to 'clarify our existing ads policy that was intended to prohibit third party ad networks from selling burned in video and display ads on Twitch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should avoid burned-in third-party ad networks and be aware that Twitch may limit certain kinds of embedded sponsor placements; however, direct sponsorship relationships and many common sponsorship uses are not intended to be limited by the clarified policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: AutoMod and semi-automated moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch announced a semi-automated chat moderation tool (AutoMod), which uses natural language processing and machine learning to set aside potentially unwanted content for human review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamers should be aware that chat content and possibly some stream content may be flagged automatically for review; maintain chat/moderation practices to reduce false positives and harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety Advisory Council role and moderation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch introduced a Safety Advisory Council made up from streamers, academics, and think tanks, with a goal to develop guidelines for moderation, work-life balance, and safeguarding marginalized communities; Twitch clarified the council's role was purely advisory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guidance may be informed by advisory groups but is ultimately enforced by Twitch; streamers should follow official Community Guidelines and platform enforcement rather than assume advisory recommendations are binding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream categorization and allowed content categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch added official categories for music streams, Creative (for artistic/creative works), an IRL category designed for content within Twitch guidelines that does not fall within established categories, and other categories (e.g., Social eating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streams must be placed in appropriate categories and should comply with category-specific norms and Twitch's broader Community Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-tagging and accessibility tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch announced introduction of over 350 new tags to categorize streams, including finer tags for gender identity, sexual identity, and disabilities, developed in consultation with charities and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of descriptive tags helps viewers find content and supports accessibility; streamers should apply accurate tags (including identity/accessibility tags) as appropriate and consult guidance from partnered organizations if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and incident response practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Following unauthorized access to user information, Twitch reset all user passwords and disabled all connections to external Twitter and YouTube accounts. Twitch also reset all stream keys as a precaution after a later data leak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamers should be prepared to rotate stream keys, secure linked accounts, and follow platform security advisories in response to breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual streaming-hour obligations in exclusivity deals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reportedly, YouTube's exclusivity contracts start at 100 hours of streaming time per month while Twitch's start at 200 hours of streaming time per month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering exclusivity deals, creators must evaluate workload and work–life balance obligations implicit in hourly commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling-related content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch announced 'slots and roulette gambling ban' and has 'cracked down on gambling' content, indicating restrictions on gambling activities on the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamers should avoid streaming unapproved gambling or gambling-promotion activities; Twitch's policy enforcement in this area has been active and evolving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emote moderation and removal precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch removed the PogChamp emote in January 2021 in response to comments from the streamer Ryan 'Gootecks' Gutierrez supporting civil unrest; Twitch later used rotating replacements and then elected a permanent replacement (KomodoHype).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand assets (emotes) may be removed for conduct considered harmful or inconsistent with platform standards; communities may be consulted for replacements, but the platform retains final authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional service limitations and compliance (example: South Korea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch announced it would stop operating in South Korea because of its network fee policy; prior to this Twitch had restricted streams to 720p quality in September 2022 and blocked access to video-on-demand content in February 2023 for South Korean users, and said users in South Korea would no longer be allowed to monetize their streams or remain in affiliate/partnership programs. In February 2024 Twitch was fined by the Korea Telecommunications Commission over service degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local regulatory, network, and commercial conditions can lead to region-specific constraints on stream quality, VOD access, and monetization; creators should monitor regional policy changes affecting their audience and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform engineering trade-offs affecting interactivity (latency vs buffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Twitch implemented a new video system, it was initially criticized because it caused a significant stream delay, interfering with broadcaster–viewer interaction; staff said increased delay was likely temporary and an acceptable trade-off for decreased buffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical changes can alter viewer–broadcaster interactivity (latency), so creators should be aware that platform-level engineering decisions may affect real-time engagement and adapt content/interaction strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner program perks and qualification implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Partner Program allows popular content producers to share in advertisement revenue and provides perks (subscriptions, emotes, live chat privileges, and other perks). The program launched in July 2011 and scaled over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becoming a partner confers monetization and community features but also carries program-specific rules and expectations; creators should understand partner obligations before pursuing partnership.
